newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican avocado growers await lifting of U.S. ban.
newsitem.headline: Mexican avocado growers await lifting of U.S. ban.

text.p: Banned from selling their product to the United States for more than 80 years, Mexican avocado growers said they finally expect to export north of the border in December, following the U.S. presidential elections.

"We're hoping for a favorable ruling ... now is an important moment politically because nobody wants to make waves until after the elections," Enrique Bautista Villegas, president of the Michoacan Avocado Commission, told Reuters in an interview.
The wait has been a long one. In 1914, the United States banned the sale of Mexican avocados, arguing that worms in the Mexican growing regions endangered U.S. produce.
The ban continued despite the 1993 signing of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).
But Bautista said it has more to do with politics than pests, benefitting U.S. growers who have been shielded from cheaper imports from Mexico.
"Our crops have never been affected," he said. "Proof of that is that we have exported for 10 years to different countries around the world and we've never had a complaint."

Mexican growers said they are pinning their hopes on bilateral talks that concluded a year ago, in which they demonstrated their product was free of the "barrenador" worm, which drills into the fruit and into the branches of avocado trees.
Mexico is the leading avocado producer in the world, controlling about 45 percent of the global market. Michoacan state is the source of nearly 80 percent of Mexico's avocados.
Ricardo Salgado, manager of the Mexican Avocado Exporters Association, said California growers have been the staunchest opponents of allowing in Mexican avocados.
"They say that once we come in, that will be the end of the avocado industry," Salgado said.
Bautista said U.S. growers receive about one dollar per kilogram while Mexican avocados fetch about half that.
"We'd be doing a great business," Bautista said.
Michoacan growers have the advantage of cheaper labor and better soil, he said.

In any event, a lifting of the U.S. ban would only be partial to start with, as the year-old bilateral accords call for allowing Mexican avocados in 19 northeastern states, one Michoacan official said, asking to remain anonymous.
Moreover, the sales would limited from November to February, the offseason for California avocados, he said.
